blocks.heading_context: ## Engineering Bridge: Musical Form as Formal Grammar
blocks.text:
MUSICAL FORM                     FORMAL LANGUAGE / CS EQUIVALENT
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Section labels (A, B, C)         Terminal symbols in a grammar
Form template (ABA', ABACA)      Production rules of a context-free grammar
  Binary: S → A B                  where each rule constrains tonal state
  Ternary: S → A B A'
  Rondo: S → A B A C A (D A)*
  Sonata: S → Expo Dev Recap

Sonata form tonal plan            Finite state machine over tonal states
  States: {Tonic, Dominant,         Exposition: Tonic → Dominant
           Remote, RetransD}        Development: Dominant → Remote → RetransD
  Retransition = dominant pedal     RetransD → Tonic (fires when P-theme arrives)
  before recapitulation             Recapitulation: stay in Tonic state

Schenkerian analysis              Parse tree / AST hierarchy
  Background: I → V → I            Root of the tree (fundamental structure)
  Middleground: prolongations       Interior nodes (transformations)
  Foreground: surface events        Leaf nodes (concrete syntax)
  Reduction = stripping ornament    AST ← concrete syntax tree

blocks.heading_context: ## The Big Picture: Music as Architecture
blocks.text:
FORM = the large-scale structure — how sections relate and how the piece unfolds

DIMENSIONS OF FORM:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ THEMATIC: what melodic material appears and when                │
  │           A section, B section, returning A', new C             │
  │                                                                 │
  │ TONAL:    what keys are established and when                    │
  │           Home → related key → development → return home        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ PHRASE:   how melodic units group and balance                   │
  │           Antecedent + consequent = period (8 bars)             │
  │           4+4+8 = sentence structure (Schoenberg's terminology) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SCALE HIERARCHY:
  Motive (2–3 notes) → Figure → Phrase (4–8 bars) →
  Period (2 phrases) → Section (multiple periods) → Movement → Work

PERIOD: two contrasting phrases — antecedent + consequent
  Antecedent: opens phrase, ends with half cadence (HC) — question
  Consequent: same opening, ends with authentic cadence (PAC) — answer
  Classic 8-bar period: 4 bars antecedent + 4 bars consequent

  PARALLEL PERIOD: consequent starts same as antecedent (most common)
  CONTRASTING PERIOD: consequent starts differently

SENTENCE: motivic presentation → continuation → cadence
  Bars 1–2: BASIC IDEA (2 bars)
  Bars 3–4: REPETITION of basic idea (same, varied, or transposed)
  Bars 5–6: CONTINUATION — fragmentation, faster harmonic rhythm
  Bars 7–8: CADENTIAL — I⁶₄ → V → I (or similar)

  The sentence is inherently forward-driving (fragmentation creates momentum)
  The period is more static (balanced question/answer)

||: A :||: B :||

SIMPLE BINARY: A and B use same thematic material, B is development/continuation
  A: tonic → dominant (or relative major in minor key)
  B: starts in dominant/relative, returns to tonic
  No exact return of opening — B dissolves back to tonic

  Used in: Baroque dance forms (allemande, sarabande, gavotte, gigue, minuet)
  Length: usually 8–16 bars each section

ROUNDED BINARY: B concludes with return of A material in tonic
  A:  tonic → dominant
  B:  dominant → (development) → RETURN of A in tonic (last few bars)
  ||: A :||: B + A' :||
  The A' return is usually shorter than the original A
  This is a SEED of sonata form — the germ of the recapitulation idea

  Used in: Bach minuets, most Classical minuet/trio movements
  Transitional form between Baroque and Classical

BALANCED BINARY: The END of A returns at end of B, but in tonic
  Technically: end of A was in dominant, end of B uses same music but in tonic
  "Balanced" = matching endings in different keys

TERNARY: ||: A :|| ||: B :|| A'
  A: complete, self-contained musical statement in tonic
  B: contrasting middle section (different key, character, material)
  A': return of A, usually in tonic, often abbreviated

  The distinguishing feature vs rounded binary:
    Ternary: A is COMPLETE and self-contained (perfect authentic cadence)
    Rounded binary: A is not complete on its own

  SIMPLE TERNARY: A and B are both complete, A' = exact repeat
  COMPOUND TERNARY: A and/or B are themselves ternary or binary

  Used in: Songs, da capo arias ("dal segno al coda"), all minuet-with-trio movements
  Da capo aria: opera form where B section = new text, A' = "da capo" (from the head)

MINUET AND TRIO:
  Minuet (A): rounded binary form
  Trio (B): contrasting rounded binary, often lighter texture, different key
  Minuet (A'): repeated without internal repeats
  → Compound ternary where each section is binary

blocks.heading_context: ## 32-Bar AABA (Tin Pan Alley / Great American Songbook)
blocks.text:
AABA FORM (32 bars):
  A: 8 bars — main theme in tonic
  A: 8 bars — same theme repeated (sometimes varied)
  B: 8 bars — BRIDGE (contrasting section, different harmony/key)
  A: 8 bars — return of main theme

  Total: 32 bars = one full chorus

  The "bridge" (B section = also called "middle eight" or "release"):
    Usually modulates to a related key (IV, V, or III area)
    Higher energy or different register
    Creates contrast before final A resolution

FAMOUS AABA SONGS:
  "I Got Rhythm" (Gershwin) — the II-V progression of Rhythm changes
  "Autumn Leaves" — AABA with a slight formal twist
  "The Way You Look Tonight" — classic AABA
  "Over the Rainbow" — AABA
  "All the Things You Are" — AABCA (modified)

RHYTHM CHANGES (based on "I Got Rhythm"):
  A section (8 bars):
    B♭  G7  Cm  F7 |  B♭  B♭7  E♭  E♭m  | B♭  F7  B♭  F7 | B♭ (cadence)
  B section (bridge, 8 bars):
    D7  D7  D7  D7  | G7  G7  G7  G7 | C7  C7  C7  C7 | F7  F7  F7  F7
    (secondary dominants descending: III7 → VI7 → II7 → V7 — each 2 bars)
  → The Rhythm changes bridge = chain of secondary dominants
    Bebop musicians improvise over this at breakneck speed

THEME AND VARIATIONS (T + V1 + V2 + V3 ... + Vn):
  Theme: stated clearly, often simple binary or rounded binary
  Each variation: transforms the theme while preserving its harmonic/phrase skeleton

VARIATION TYPES:
  Melodic variation: ornament, embellish, or replace the melody
  Rhythmic variation: change note values (triplets, dotted, faster subdivision)
  Harmonic variation: add extensions, change mode (major→minor or reverse)
  Textural variation: change register, add counterpoint, change density
  Modal variation: minor → major (or reverse) = "change of mode"
  Virtuosic variation: technically demanding display
  Character variation: march, waltz, fugue, siciliana (dance variation)
  Finale: usually a grand, fast-tempo conclusion ("finale" variation)

FAMOUS EXAMPLES:
  Bach: Goldberg Variations (30 variations on aria, every 3rd = canon at wider interval)
  Beethoven: Diabelli Variations (33 variations, the pianistic summit)
  Brahms: Variations on a Theme by Handel, Paganini
  Mozart: Piano Sonata K. 331 (theme + 6 variations, ends with "Rondo alla turca")

SONATA FORM — THREE-PART ARCH:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ EXPOSITION      │ DEVELOPMENT        │ RECAPITULATION            │
  │ (Establish)     │ (Destabilize)      │ (Resolve)                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       ||:                                                         :||
       (repeated)                                             (to coda)

EXPOSITION:
  PRIMARY THEME (P): First theme group, in TONIC key
    Usually strong, assertive character
    Establishes home tonality definitively

  TRANSITION (TR): Modulates from tonic to new key
    Rising energy, harmonic motion
    Ends with "medial caesura" — a pause before 2nd theme

  SECONDARY THEME (S): Second theme group, in SECONDARY key
    Major key: secondary = DOMINANT (V)
    Minor key: secondary = RELATIVE MAJOR (♭III)
    Usually contrasting character (if P is forte, S may be piano)

  CLOSING THEME/CODETTA (K): Confirms secondary key
    Cadential figures, closure-signaling material
    Sometimes generates most memorable tunes (e.g., Beethoven Op. 18 No. 1)

DEVELOPMENT:
  Works with material from exposition (P, TR, S, K, or new material)
  Operations: fragmentation, sequence, modulation, imitation, inversion
  Typically moves through many keys (remote from home)
  Creates maximum instability, harmonic tension
  Ends with RETRANSITION: sustained dominant pedal, building to recapitulation

RECAPITULATION:
  Returns to TONIC key — the resolution of the development's instability
  P: returns in tonic (same as exposition)
  TR: modified — no longer needs to modulate; stays in tonic
  S: returns in TONIC (crucial difference from exposition — 2nd theme now in home key)
  K: in tonic

CODA:
  Optional but common extension after recapitulation
  Can be short (confirming tonic) or massive development in itself
  Beethoven's codas are often as long as the development
  Provides final structural affirmation of tonic

EXPOSITION:         DEVELOPMENT:        RECAPITULATION:
  P: TONIC            remote keys           P: TONIC
  S: DOMINANT         dominant pedal        S: TONIC ← KEY DIFFERENCE
                    ↗                    ↙
    ─────────────────── home ──────────────────
    The arc:   LEAVE     →   WANDER    →   RETURN

The fundamental "narrative arc" of sonata form:
  Tension (departure to dominant) → Crisis (development) → Resolution (return)

CLASSICAL CONCERTO FIRST MOVEMENT (modified sonata):
  ORCHESTRAL EXPOSITION: orchestra alone
    P in tonic, S in TONIC (not dominant — orchestra stays home)
    Introduces all themes, but no modulation to dominant
    This creates expectation: where will the soloist go?

  SOLO EXPOSITION: soloist enters
    P with soloist (orchestra accompanies)
    S in DOMINANT (now the modulation happens — the soloist goes out)
    This is the "real" exposition in functional terms

  DEVELOPMENT: soloist + orchestra
  RECAPITULATION: P and S both in tonic
  CADENZA: soloist alone (improvised originally, written out later)
    Typically on the I⁶₄ chord before final V → I
    Free fantasy on the movement's themes
    Ends with trill → orchestra resumes for final bars

CLASSICAL/ROMANTIC SYMPHONY:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ MVT I     Fast        Sonata form      Tonic key     Weighty   │
  │ MVT II    Slow        Ternary/Sonata   Related key   Lyrical   │
  │ MVT III   Moderate    Minuet + Trio    Tonic         Dance     │
  │           (or Scherzo)                                         │
  │ MVT IV    Fast        Rondo/Sonata     Tonic key     Brilliant │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Beethoven innovations:
  Mvt III: Minuet → Scherzo (faster, more vigorous — from Haydn 3/4 dance to Beethoven 3/4 sprint)
  Mvt IV: sometimes cyclic (returns themes from earlier movements — Beethoven 5th, 9th)
  Beethoven 9th: choral finale — breaks out of instrumental form entirely

Brahms: longer development sections, more motivic unity across movements
Mahler: symphony as world — 60-90 minutes, multiple extra movements, expanded orchestra
